subsystems.name: Opsin gene payload
subsystems.role: the light-sensitive protein that makes a neuron respond to light.

subsystems.name: Viral vector
subsystems.role: delivers the opsin gene into the target cells.

subsystems.name: Light delivery
subsystems.role: shines light of the correct wavelength onto the modified cells.
parts: external goggles (for retinal therapy) or implanted connector (for brain)

subsystems.name: Control and power unit
subsystems.role: drives the light source with precise timing, intensity and pulse patterns.

subsystems.name: Surgical targeting system
subsystems.role: places the vector and any implanted hardware accurately and safely.
parts: stereotactic frame or retinal surgical tools

buildSteps.title: Select target and opsin
buildSteps.detail: Identify the specific neuron type to control and choose an opsin with the right light wavelength, speed and effect (excitation or inhibition).

buildSteps.title: Design the gene cassette
buildSteps.detail: Combine the opsin gene with a promoter that restricts expression to the target cells, plus elements for long-term stability.

buildSteps.title: Produce the viral vector
buildSteps.detail: Package the cassette into AAV in a laboratory, then purify and titre the batch to clinical standards.

buildSteps.title: Validate in animals
buildSteps.detail: Test expression, light-evoked neural activity, behavioural effect and safety in animal models of the disorder.

buildSteps.title: Deliver the vector
buildSteps.detail: Inject the vector into the target tissue — into the eye for retinal disease, or into a specific brain region for neurological disorders.

buildSteps.title: Implant or apply the light device
buildSteps.detail: For the eye, provide light-stimulating goggles that project patterned light onto the retina; for the brain, surgically implant a fibre-optic or LED probe.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate stimulation
buildSteps.detail: Adjust light intensity, pulse width and frequency to produce the desired therapeutic effect without damaging tissue.

buildSteps.title: Monitor and follow up
buildSteps.detail: Track neural response, immune reaction and clinical benefit over months to years, adjusting treatment as needed.

prerequisites.why: approved gene therapies for inherited blindness already use AAV to deliver genes to retinal cells safely.
decades of neuroscience research show that opsins can control specific neurons with light in living animals.
some promoters work well in animals, but few are validated to target precise human neuron types without off-target effects.
fibre optics and LEDs work in animals for weeks, but long-term safe human implants for deep brain use are still experimental.
the vector and light device must avoid immune rejection and tissue damage for years in human patients.
optogenetic therapy combines a biologic and a device, so approval requires coordinated evidence across both.

pathway.milestone: early clinical trials in inherited blindness (e.g. retinitis pigmentosa) using optogenetic therapy
pathway.unlocks: first proof that the approach can restore some visual function in humans.

pathway.milestone: refined light-delivery goggles and broader retinal disease trials
pathway.unlocks: a potential commercial therapy for certain forms of blindness.

pathway.milestone: preclinical and early trials for brain disorders such as epilepsy or Parkinson's disease using implanted fibre optics
pathway.unlocks: a new option for drug-resistant neurological conditions.

pathway.milestone: closed-loop optogenetic systems that read and write neural activity in real time
pathway.unlocks: precise, adaptive neuromodulation for psychiatric and movement disorders.
